column1: What is the fundamental physics paradox of countersteering?
column2: To turn right, the rider must first push the right handlebar forward (steering the front wheel left), which initiates a lean to the right; the lean angle then generates the centripetal force needed for cornering.

column1: What is the lean angle equilibrium equation for a motorcycle in steady-state cornering?
column2: tan(φ) = v²/(r·g), where φ is lean angle from vertical, v is speed, r is corner radius, and g is gravitational acceleration. Notably, this is independent of mass.

column1: Why do a 90 kg superbike and a 190 kg adventure tourer require the same lean angle at identical speed and radius?
column2: Lean angle equilibrium depends only on v²/(r·g), not mass—the heavier machine generates proportionally greater lateral force but also greater gravitational restoring torque, so the geometric lean angle required is identical.

column1: What three geometric parameters primarily govern motorcycle steering feel and self-centering?
column2: Trail (horizontal distance between steering axis ground intersection and tire contact patch, producing self-centering torque), fork rake angle (modulates trail and steering effort), and chassis mass distribution/CG location.

column1: What are the three distinct stability regimes of a motorcycle across speed ranges?
column2: 1) Parking lot speeds: near-zero self-stability, requires constant rider correction. 2) Urban/moderate speeds: capsize stability—tendency to self-correct from small disturbances, but still needs active input. 3) Highway speeds: gyroscopic effects dominate, strong resistance to steering inputs and external disturbances.

column1: What slip angle range typically produces peak lateral tire friction coefficient?
column2: Approximately 4 to 12 degrees of slip angle produces peak lateral force generation before friction coefficient degrades with further slip.

column1: What slip ratio range typically produces peak longitudinal tire friction coefficient?
column2: Approximately 8 to 15 percent slip ratio produces peak longitudinal force generation before the tire transitions into diminishing returns and eventual slide.

column1: What two molecular-scale mechanisms compete to produce the tire's peak-then-decline friction characteristic?
column2: Adhesion (intermolecular bonding between rubber and asphalt, dominant at low slip) and hysteresis (viscoelastic energy dissipation via internal friction, which increases with slip rate and generates heat that alters compound properties).

column1: How does longitudinal load transfer during acceleration scale, and what amplifies it?
column2: Load transfer magnitude scales linearly with acceleration magnitude and with the ratio of center-of-mass height to wheelbase length; a high CG or short wheelbase amplifies the effect, increasing rear load and unloading the front tire.

column1: Why does a motorcycle's high-speed lean-initiated turn differ fundamentally from a car's cornering mechanism?
column2: A car corners while remaining upright, generating lateral force at the contact patch with chassis roll against suspension; a motorcycle corners by falling—the rider initiates a controlled lean/topple toward the turn's inside, and the lean angle itself is the cornering force vector made visible.

column1: What does the friction circle (or friction ellipse) represent for a motorcycle tire, and why is it critical to combined braking/cornering?
column2: It represents the total friction force available at the contact patch in any direction; since lateral (cornering) and longitudinal (braking/accel) forces share the same finite friction budget, increasing lean angle consumption leaves less grip available for simultaneous braking or throttle input.

column1: What minimum sampling rate and sensor channels does a typical MoTeC ADL3 motorcycle data logger capture?
column2: Minimum 100 Hz sampling across wheel speed sensors, fork/shock suspension linear potentiometers, brake line hydraulic pressure transducers, throttle position, engine RPM (ignition coil inductive pickup), GPS velocity/lateral acceleration, and a six-axis IMU (roll, pitch, yaw rate, tri-axial accelerometer).
